slides.title: How Tight Is the Cloud?
slides.alt: A scatter diagram of twenty points rising in a tight cloud

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the cloud? · The situation
slides.title: Revision and marks

setup.preamble: A teacher wonders whether students who revise more score higher on the unit test.
setup.para: She asks 20 students how many hours they revise each week, $x$, and records each test mark out of $100$, $y$. Every student is one point on a scatter diagram.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the cloud? · Question 1
slides.title: Read the cloud
slides.stem: Predict: which value of $r$ matches this scatter diagram?

walk.cap: The points hug a rising line
walk.note: The correlation coefficient $r$ is found on the GDC. A value near $1$ means a tight, rising, straight pattern.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the cloud? · Question 1
slides.title: A scale for $|r|$
slides.stem: How do we put a word on the size of $r$? Use $|r|$, the size without the sign.

walk.note: The sign gives the direction: $+$ rises, $-$ falls. This scatter is a very strong positive correlation.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the cloud? · Question 2
slides.title: Spread the points
slides.stem: A second school finds the same trend, but the points are more spread out. Predict what happens to $r$.

walk.note: $r$ falls as the points spread out. It stays positive because the trend still rises.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the cloud? · Spread the points
slides.title: Spread and correlation
A Curve That Only Goes Up
slides.alt: A plant’s height each week: points rising along an upward curve

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · The situation
slides.title: A seedling

setup.preamble: A gardener measures a seedling at the end of each week.
setup.para: Over 10 weeks she records $x$, the week number, and $y$, the height in centimetres. The plant is taller every week than the week before.

facts.html: 10 weeks of heights: one point each

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Question 1
slides.title: Always rising
slides.stem: Predict: the plant rises every week. What is $r$?

walk.cap: Always rising, but not a line
walk.note: A relationship that only rises, or only falls, is monotonic. $r$ only rewards a straight line, so it stays below $1$.

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Question 2
slides.title: One odd point
slides.stem: A sensor glitch records the plant at only $5$ cm in week 11. Predict what happens to $r$.

walk.note: One unusual point, an outlier, can drag $r$ a long way.

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Drag the outlier
slides.title: One point and correlation
Eight Sprinters
slides.alt: Eight athletes: a rising scatter that levels off

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · The situation
slides.title: Training and improvement

setup.preamble: A coach follows eight sprinters through a season.
setup.para: For each athlete she records $x$, the hours of training each week, and $y$, how many seconds faster the athlete runs 100 m. More training helps, but the gains slow down.

facts.html: $y$: improvement in 100 m time, in seconds

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 1
slides.title: Rank by hand
slides.stem: On paper, rank $x$ and $y$, smallest first. Two athletes tie on $y$: what rank does each get?

walk.note: The tied athletes share places 3 and 4, so each takes the average, $\frac{3+4}{2}=3.5$.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 2
slides.title: Which is larger?
slides.stem: Next the GDC finds $r$ for the data, then the same calculation on the ranks. Predict which is larger.

walk.note: First $r$ for the data, then $r$ for the ranks. The second is called Spearman’s $r_s$.

slides.title: Find $r$ for the data
slides.stem: Hours $x$ are in List 1 and improvements $y$ in List 2.

start.alt: List 1 holds the hours and List 2 the improvements

steps.t: Press [F6] SET. 2Var XList is List 1 and 2Var YList is List 2.

slides.title: Find $r_s$ from the ranks
slides.stem: Your ranks of $x$ are in List 3 and your ranks of $y$ in List 4. The tied ranks are $3.5$.

start.alt: Ranks entered in List 3 and List 4; the CALC menu is open

steps.t: Press [F6] SET. [DOWN] twice, [F1] LIST, {3} [EXE] for 2Var XList. Then [DOWN], [F1] LIST, {4} [EXE] for 2Var YList.
Press [F1] ax+b. Read $r_s=0.994$ to 3 s.f. Afterwards set SET back to List 1 and List 2.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 3
slides.title: What does $r_s>r$ suggest?
slides.stem: The GDC gives $r=0.935$ and $r_s=0.994$. What does $r_s>r$ suggest?

walk.note: It suggests the data rise steadily but along a curve, or an outlier is dragging $r$ down. Always check the scatter.

choices: A steady rise along a curve

Ice Cream and Sunburn
slides.alt: Twelve months of ice cream sales against sunburn cases: a rising band

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · The situation
slides.title: A coastal town

setup.preamble: A seaside town keeps two records through the year.
setup.para: Each month it notes $x$, the ice creams sold per day, and $y$, the sunburn cases seen at the clinic. That gives 12 points.

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · Question 1
slides.title: Cause?
slides.stem: The scatter has $r=0.99$. Does eating ice cream cause sunburn?

walk.cap: A high $r$ is not a cause
walk.note: Correlation says the variables move together. It never says that one causes the other.

choices: Yes: a high $r$ shows one causes the other
No: they have nothing to do with each other
They move together, but $r$ cannot say why

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · Question 2
slides.title: A third variable
slides.stem: Something else changes through the year. What could be behind both?

walk.note: Hot months have more ice cream and more sunburn: the weather drives both. A third variable can produce a strong $r$.
